newsitem.title: UK: OECD sees solid Finnish growth but urges vigilance.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees solid Finnish growth but urges vigilance.

text.p: The Finnish economy is projected to grow by four percent both in 1997 and 1998 and monetary authorities will need to remain vigilant on the inflation front, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said on Friday.
In a report originally scheduled for Monday, the OECD said wage and price inflation should remain modest at three percent and two percent respectively in 1998.
The report's embargo was lifted on Friday after information from the report was published ahead of schedule.
"While there seem to be favourable prospects for sustained growth, monetary policy should guard against a possible revival of inflation," the OECD said.

"A further strengthening of domestic demand, with buoyant household consumption, rising residential investment and sustained business investment" were seen as the main driving forces behind the expanding economy.

"Foreign demand should also stay resilient as exports are expected to benefit from the stronger expansion envisaged in Europe," it said. "Unemployment is therefore projected to decline further, reaching 13-1/2 percent in 1998."

The OECD said that if there were higher wage claims in some sectors of the economy, there was a risk they could spread to other sectors and generate pressure on domestic prices. That, it said, had been the case in previous upswings.
"The monetary authorities need, therefore, to remain vigilant to a possible resurgence of inflation."
Finland's easy monetary policy -- allowed because inflation targets have been achieved comfortably -- has counteracted upward pressure on the markka, it said.

"Should these pressures persist, monetary policy might be faced with the dilemma of either keeping the emphasis on exchange rate stability, but with the risk of undermining inflation control, or leaving the markka to appreciate within the wider bands of the ERM," it said.
That, it added, could adversely affect the competitiveness and, in turn, labour demand of highly exposed export manufacturing industries.
